Separate normalization does not generally make branch allocation affect only variance. For branch b with n IID sequences, let G_i be summed token gradients and C_i valid-target counts; its gradient estimator is ĝ_b=ΣG_i/ΣC_i. Applying classical ratio-estimator analysis componentwise gives E[ĝ_b]≈r_b+[r_b Var(C)−Cov(G,C)]/[n(E[C])²], where r_b=E[G]/E[C]. Thus changing branch batch size can change expected gradients through finite-sample bias; the direction depends on count–gradient dependence. This is an application of the Taylor-expansion analysis in [Shalabh’s ratio-estimation notes](https://home.iitk.ac.in/~shalab/sampling/chapter5-sampling-ratio-method-estimation.pdf), assuming positive denominators and suitable moments.

Variable-length token normalization creates a related distinction: averaging separately normalized microbatch losses differs from summing losses and dividing by the combined target count. [Hugging Face’s analysis](https://huggingface.co/blog/gradient_accumulation) documents this explicitly. Pooling counts reproduces the realized full-batch token mean, but does not automatically eliminate population ratio-estimator bias. [Ogliore et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.0797) similarly demonstrate, for counting measurements, why averaging more small ratios need not remove their bias, whereas pooling counts reduces it.

For fixed coefficients λ₁,λ₂, allocation preserves expected raw-gradient weighting only if each branch estimator’s expectation is allocation-independent. Sufficient conditions include fixed counts per sequence, or E[G_i|C_i]=C_i g_b with unchanged sampling and masking distributions. Random counts alone therefore do not prove bias. Zero-target handling, length-dependent gradient means, or allocation-dependent sampling can break invariance. These statements concern gradients at fixed parameters; nonlinear clipping and adaptive optimizers can change expected parameter updates even when mean gradients agree.
